lines.5501: ### 6.4.1 Stage A: full-state exchange of the ban
lines.5503: We call a *full-state exchange* the replacement, in the forward pass of the neutral twin, of the residual states at a set of positions and blocks by the states the full ban prompt produces at the same positions; because the twin and the ban have identical token ids from the task text on, every task-specification position aligns. The exchanges covered four block bands at the task-specification positions (0 to 11, 12 to 23, 24 to 35, 0 to 35), a splice of the key-value cache of the condition span (the direct route), and the read position at all 36 blocks. The controls were the twin, a matched-norm random exchange (the state of the twin plus a fresh random direction scaled to the displacement that the ban itself causes per slot, block and position), a placebo that takes a second neutral twin as the source, and an identity exchange. The outcome is the share of correct programs implementing the substitute Y of the ban; the *transfer* of a cell is its Y share minus that of the twin, and its *recovery* is the transfer divided by that of the full ban. Each cell has N = 30 on paired slots. Tables 244 to 249 give every cell on the six tasks.
lines.5505: The prediction held where the route data said it should, and failed at one task where they said it should not. On shortest path, exchanging the full ban's task-specification states at all blocks into the twin turns 24 of 30 slots from Dijkstra to Bellman-Ford/SPFA (transfer 0.80, McNemar 24:0, Holm p 7e-7, pass ratio 0.90), while the condition-span splice and the read-position exchange transfer nothing. Blocks 12 to 23 alone carry 0.60 and blocks 24 to 35 alone 0.37; blocks 0 to 11 carry none. On kth smallest the same exchange transfers 0.57 to quickselect with every slot leaving the full sort, blocks 0 to 11 alone already transfer 0.40, and here the condition span also carries the ban (0.93). On connected components every slot leaves union find under the exchange at blocks 12 to 23 or 0 to 35 (off-default transfer 1.00), but only 0.37 to 0.47 land on the ban's BFS and the rest on DFS. On the grid task, whose route was carried by the prompt states in likelihood and mixed in behaviour, the exchange at all blocks transfers 0.47 toward DFS and the condition-span splice 0.33, so each carries part of the ban. On the direct-route tasks the condition-span splice alone reproduces the ban (two sum 1.00, find duplicate 0.90), as predicted, but on two sum the task-specification states also transfer brute force at 0.43, above the predicted ceiling of 0.2. The committed verdict is therefore not supported. The secondary predictions hold: the condition span carries at least 0.5 on the direct-route tasks and at most 0.2 on shortest path, the read position carries at most 0.2 everywhere (it carries 0.00 on all six tasks), the placebo moves at most 0.03, and the exchange beats the matched-norm random exchange where it transfers (shortest path 23:0, kth smallest 16:2, connected components 11:0). The ban's information, not the size of the perturbation, is what moves the algorithm.

lines.5775: ## 6.5 Gemma: a one-token fork, and Gemma Scope 2 features against difference in means
lines.5777: **Why Gemma.** Asked one and the same grid-path prompt, gemma-3-4b-it [76] writes DFS about 70% of the time and BFS about 30%, so it offers what Qwen3-8B never does: the request's BFS-against-DFS contrast inside one prompt, with no ban or instruction to confound it. Gemma Scope 2 provides sparse autoencoders on the residual stream after each block, trained on this instruct model, so the feature claim needs no transfer test. Qwen-3 transcoders for circuit tracing exist as well [123], but they would have to study a choice Qwen3-8B does not make naturally. The experiment [ARTIFACT:art_zNyBP6zieI5u] asked where the choice forks, whether it can be read from the internals beyond what the visible text already says, and whether the SAE features steer it better than plain baselines: a difference-in-means direction, the raw residual, random features, isotropic directions, DAS and prompting. It used the residual-stream SAEs at layers 9, 17, 22 and 29 (16k latents, at the release's medium sparsity), one 16 GB card and exact common random numbers, under two hash-chained commitments.

lines.5837: **Steering: the features move the fork, difference in means moves it more, and every fork edit breaks programs.** We call an *SAE clamp* setting the k latents that best separate forced-BFS from forced-DFS prompts (input-selected) to their BFS-class mean at the fork position; output-scored latents are chosen instead by their attribution to the fork's logit difference, and the two sets of 20 share 2 latents. At the fork position of layer 22, edits at matched norm moved y by +4.04 nats for the difference-in-means direction, +1.78 for the SAE clamp of the top 20 input-selected latents, +0.51 for 20 random latents and +0.12 for an isotropic direction. Table 261b gives the whole dose-response sweep over the 120 prompt variants (11,280 measurements), at the fork and at the task-specification positions. In generation (N = 50 paired slots), the twin wrote BFS in 13 programs; the SAE clamp raised this to 30 (top 20 latents) and 36 (top 50), the difference-in-means edit at the same norm to 46 and 49, and random latents to 21 (Table 262). Every edit at the fork lowered the pass rate, from 0.84 for the twin to 0.58 and 0.48 for the SAE clamps and 0.32 and 0.16 for difference in means, so the preregistered outcome, correct BFS programs, shows no significant effect anywhere after Holm correction, and no feature claim is made. The preregistered feature rule (SAE target-correct count at least the difference-in-means count, at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the twin's) is also met by random latents at k = 50 (9 against 7, pass 0.76), so it cannot discriminate here. The informative comparisons are on attempted BFS, and they are descriptive: the SAE clamp beats the twin (17:0 and 23:0 discordant slots, p 1.5e-5 and 2.4e-7) and random latents (15:0, p 6.1e-5), and difference in means beats the SAE clamp at matched norm (16:0, p 3.1e-5). At matched effect on y rather than matched norm, difference in means and the SAE clamp shift the plan equally (32 against 30 BFS, p 0.50; 34 against 36, p 0.63) and difference in means keeps slightly more programs correct (13 against 9, 14 against 10). Edits at the task-specification positions do nothing (12 to 19 BFS against 13). Steering toward DFS works cleanly for both (SAE 47 of 50, difference in means 50 of 50, against 37 for the twin; pass 0.98 to 1.00). Difference-in-means steering of a code model's choice of language and library has shown the same trade-off, with overly strong interventions reducing output quality [130]. AxBench found simple baselines ahead of SAE steering [34], and a 2026 reanalysis puts SAEs close to AxBench's reference when latents are selected and labelled by a supervised pipeline [131]; here, at comparable norms, neither the input-selected nor the output-scored clamp reached the difference-in-means edit (Table 261b).

lines.5935: ## 6.6 The plan in words: a natural language autoencoder on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
lines.5937: **Why.** The request names NLA as an instrument, and the release of NLA checkpoints for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] made it possible to ask, in words, whether the residual stream states before the first code token say which algorithm will be written. The experiment [ARTIFACT:art_dbUtqBjT0tPf] read layer-20 states with the released verbalizer and reconstructor pair, judged the explanations blind, and tested an edit of the explanation as a steering vector. Published verbalizers of the same kind include LatentQA [117] and SelfIE [118], and a 2026 analysis of a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer found that only a small share of an explanation's specific claims are ones the reconstruction depends on [119]. Pre-registration was a sha256 chain of four commitments, each preceding its samples; the parts added after the committed nulls are marked exploratory.

lines.5962: **The NLA never names the planned algorithm before the code.** Two blind judges from different families (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite and Mistral Small 3.2, both scoring 1.00 on calibration; a third model resolved 1,064 disagreements) mapped each of 6,180 explanations to a catalogue algorithm or to none named (Table 269). Every preregistered readout at the end-of-prompt positions is exactly zero (Table 270). On ban prompts, explanations named the substitute in 0 of 16 states (only two sum had a substitute, so this test is underpowered); on twin prompts they named the default in 0 of 112, as did the text-only reader; on ban failures they named the default the model still writes in 0 of 96. The positive control failed too: on forced `Implement Y` prompts the explanations called Y planned in 0 of 7 tasks, while the text-only reader did so on all of them, and they mentioned the algorithm named in the prompt in 0.7% of cases. The explanations describe the local format line, such as a request for no explanation or a Python code block to follow, and confabulate the task (Fibonacci, medians, prime numbers); 4,733 of 5,700 judged explanations name no algorithm at all. lines.5984: **The information is local and fades within a sentence (exploratory).** To tell an instrument limit from information that fades along the prompt, the same NLA and judges read states at the token that names the algorithm inside the condition sentence and at the final period of that sentence (220 states, 660 explanations; Table 271). The null therefore says that the pre-code positions do not carry the algorithm choice in a form this NLA puts into words, not that the instrument is blind.

lines.6016: **At the generated-token site and large doses, the verbal edit steers two of four tasks (exploratory).** After the committed nulls, the experiment extended the doses and moved the edit to the read position plus generated tokens 1 to 64 (Tables 274 and 275). On find duplicate the edit at dose 8 (about 0.3 of the state norm at each position) raised Floyd cycle detection from 0.28 to 0.76 (25:1 over 50 paired slots), replicated on fresh slots (15 of 20, 13:0, p 2e-4), and beat a matched random push (28:1), an unrelated-word edit built the same way (12:1, p 0.003) and a norm-matched round trip (13:1, p 0.002); at dose 16 the programs broke (pass 0.37). On two sum brute force rose from 0 to 10 of 50 at dose 8 and to 23 of 30 at dose 16 with a pass rate of 0.90, while the random push never moved it. On connected components only the forced-state difference in means steered (union find 0.80 at dose 16, 15:1); on substring search nothing steered short of breaking the program. The prefill site stayed inert even at dose 16 or at the natural norm of the difference in means. Asking for the algorithm in the prompt remained the ceiling (forced adherence 0.90 to 1.00 on all four tasks), as the AxBench comparison of prompting and steering predicts [34]. The NLA paper itself reports that editing a plan explanation and steering at one token succeeds roughly half the time; this run's success on two of four tasks is of the same kind and is not a reliable control knob.

lines.6055: Three of the audit's flags bear on what this run may claim. No source localizes which algorithm a code model will write by interchange or DAS and validates it by scoring the generated programs, so that combination is open; the method itself is DAS. Editing an NLA explanation of a plan and steering with the reconstruction is published, so the NLA arm is a replication on a new object. Steering under quantization has been compared with full precision only for weight-only 8-bit integer and 4-bit NormalFloat quantization, with activations kept in 16-bit floating point [116]; no source found measures how dynamic per-token activation rounding changes the effect of random perturbations, which is the question the engine control answered, in the negative. The audit also recorded that community NLAs exist for Qwen3-8B at layer 24, that circuit-tracer ships Qwen-3 transcoders including 8B [123] (so the choice of Gemma for the feature claim needs its reason, which is the natural within-prompt split), and that Gemma Scope 2 dates from 22 December 2025 with instruct SAEs initialised from the pretrained ones.

lines.6182: ## 6.11 What the next iteration takes from this one
lines.6184: The plan-variable account was tested in part, and its two halves came out differently. Where the choice is held is now measured in three models: the task-specification states in Qwen3-8B for bans and instructions on the prompt-route tasks, one generated token in Gemma, and nothing verbalisable before the code in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Whether the choice is a low-rank variable in Qwen3-8B, and whether random pushes act through it, is untested, because the DAS experiment was lost at planning. The engine control has removed the obstacle that made such a test look premature: random pushes at iteration 4's absolute unit move the algorithm in bf16 as they did in 8-bit floating point, so the escapes are a stable target that a fitted plan subspace can be asked to explain. The next measurements are DAS at the task-specification positions of shortest path and kth smallest, with the Stage A exchanges as the full-state ceiling, and the projection of iteration 4's 40 directions onto the fitted subspace.
lines.6186: Three leads come with it. The ban-free unit moves fewer programs than the ban unit at a larger scalar dose, so its per-position and per-block profile, or the direction seeds, decide movability; a controlled comparison of the two units on the same seeds would say which. Gemma's one-token fork offers a clean site where DAS already captures the choice in one direction; whether a smaller push there switches the algorithm without breaking the program is the question for a usable knob. And two sum's task-specification states carry part of a ban that iteration 3 had classed as direct, so the route classes are not all-or-none.
lines.6188: # What we have learned so far
lines.6190: After six iterations the run has a firm picture of the collapse, a complete answer on temperature, a confirmed internal handle on the algorithm in Qwen3-8B, a measured map of where three models hold the choice, a measured but incomplete account of what a prohibition does, and no correct novel algorithm. Qwen3-8B [5] writes BFS and Dijkstra almost without exception on the two path search tasks and one algorithm on each of 13 further coding tasks (modal share 1.00 on 12, 0.98 on one). The collapse is not universal: three of 15 new tasks are already mixed in the instruct twin (trapped rain water, default share 0.64; minimum spanning tree weight, 0.66; valid anagram, 0.76), and on two of them the instruct model is more diverse than its base model (twin off-default 0.36 against a base off-default share of 0.23, and 0.34 against 0.11). Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [22] attempts more algorithms but its correct grid programs are BFS 20 of 20; gemma-3-4b-it [76] writes DFS in 70% and BFS in 30% of programs for one grid prompt; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] shares most of Qwen3-8B's defaults.
lines.6192: Sampling temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p, thinking mode and random context seeds change how the code is worded, not which algorithm it implements. With the token seed coupled across temperatures from 0.3 to 1.3, the algorithm changed in 0 of 20 seeds on three tasks with thinking off, and in 0 of 20 on the shortest path task with thinking on, under top-p 1 and under top-k 10. Phrasings per idea rose from 3 to 13 clusters on the grid task with thinking off; in the literal cell with thinking on, the clusters rise only at temperature 1.3 (5/7/12 at Jaccard thresholds 0.7/0.8/0.9, against 3/6/10 for a repeat at 0.7). State noise on generated tokens against a temperature matched on per-token KL was not established in bf16 (12:6 and 7:3 discordant flips). On other problems temperature above 1 has been reported to raise algorithmic diversity at a correctness cost [72], so the null belongs to these tasks.
lines.6194: A random displacement of the task-specification states at early to middle blocks, sized to the displacement a ban itself causes, changes the algorithm, and this is a property of Qwen3-8B, not of the 8-bit engine on which it was found. At iteration 4's own absolute displacement, directions and slots, bf16 escapes on 26 of 40 directions on connected components and 6 of 40 on shortest path, against 29 and 8 under the 8-bit W8A8 engine, with the same directions escaping (Spearman of per-direction shares 0.96 and 0.87), and per-sample plan noise moves 25 and 22 of 50 attempts against 30 and 22. Rounding the activations to e4m3 per token adds nothing; a 5-point per-slot boost on connected components comes from the 8-bit floating-point weights or the native kernel. The smaller effects that iteration 5 measured in bf16 belong to its ban-free dose unit or its direction seeds: its alpha-2 push was larger at the first edited block than the control's alpha-1 push, which still moved 7 of 50. In bf16 at the ban-free unit, noise at the task-specification positions moves the algorithm (kth smallest 0.37 correct off-default at alpha 2 through blocks 12 to 23; connected components 0.33 at alpha 4 through blocks 0 to 11), while the read position and the condition span barely do; the preregistered site rule was withdrawn for lack of common support and breakage at alpha 8, and a post-hoc model at alpha 4 or less puts the read position below the task-specification site on both tasks. Noise in generated tokens 1 to 32 also redirects the choice. The 8-bit site odds ratio (5.72) and the same-seed contrast (17.25 of 20 seeds) were not rerun in bf16.
lines.6196: Priced as a knob, plan noise is not the practical answer on the evidence so far. Under the 8-bit engine at the ban unit it was the cheapest route to a second correct algorithm on kth smallest (Hill-1 2.72 within 5 pass points) and connected components (2.09); fixed random directions reached above 2 at no cost on kth smallest and two sum, but as maxima over 21 and 9 directions. Against text-level plan samplers, measured in bf16 at the ban-free unit where plan noise was weak, plan noise matched the best sampler on 1 of 5 decisive tasks: an intent sentence written by the base model, with the code written by the instruct model, won on connected components, the shortest path task and two sum (2.53, 1.45 and 1.61), and enumerate and pick reached the most raw diversity at 16 to 62 pass points. That comparison has not been repeated at the absolute unit at which plan noise is strong. Plan noise beat decoding at matched departure on kth smallest at alpha 2 (13:0) and not elsewhere (6:3). Generate then select [43] and enumerate and pick, which hand the choice to an external random draw, remain ceilings with large pass costs.
lines.6198: Where the choice is held has now been measured in three models, and each location fits the behaviour of that model. In Qwen3-8B the residual states at the task-specification positions carry the substitute of a ban and the algorithm of an instruction on the prompt-route tasks: exchanging those states alone into a neutral twin transfers the ban on shortest path (0.80) and kth smallest (0.57) and a forced instruction on shortest path (30 of 30) and connected components (28 of 30), while matched-norm random exchanges and a placebo transfer at most 0.13; on the direct-route tasks the condition span carries the ban. In gemma-3-4b-it the choice between BFS and DFS is made at one generated token after a shared 32-token opening (` visited` leads to DFS with BFS probability 0.011; a blank line, `if` or `queue` lead to BFS at 0.95 to 1.00), about 138 tokens before the code identifies the algorithm. It is readable across prompts from the residual stream at that position (a preregistered Lasso on Gemma Scope 2 SAE codes R-squared 0.66 against 0.18 for the text; a post-hoc ridge on the raw state 0.72), and DAS finds it in essentially one direction (rank 1 moves the fork log-odds by 8.8 nats); a difference-in-means edit moves it 2.3 times as far as the SAE clamp at matched norm, and every edit toward the minority algorithm breaks programs, so no feature claim is made. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct a natural language autoencoder names the algorithm at the token where the prompt names it and not 170 tokens later, and its pre-code explanations name no algorithm; a verbal edit steered two of four tasks only at the generated-token site and large doses, in an exploratory follow-up. In all three models the read position is inert as a carrier. Whether the choice in Qwen3-8B is a low-rank variable, and whether random pushes act through it, is untested: the DAS experiment was lost at planning. The forced-prompt subspace of iteration 4 did not predict which directions move the algorithm (within-task Spearman 0.03), although which directions move is reproducible.
lines.6200: The internal results that hold under bf16 are therefore: the route of a ban (iterations 2 and 3), the band patching on kth smallest and connected components, the exchange of Stage A, the escape fractions and per-sample plan-noise rates of iteration 4 at their absolute unit, the transplant results of iteration 5, the read-position transplant that breaks the output without moving the algorithm, and the post-hoc ordering of noise sites. The 8-bit site odds ratio, the same-seed contrast and the forced-prompt subspace tests are 8-bit results not rerun.
lines.6202: A single prompt ban, where the model obeys it, removes the default and the output collapses on one replacement: Bellman-Ford/SPFA on the shortest path task (272 of 272 compliant iteration-1 programs; 255 of 260 iteration-2 attempts not banned), DFS on the grid task (116 of 128; 257 of 257), and quickselect and size-k heap, brute force, index marking and BFS on the bench tasks where Qwen3-8B obeys (4 of 12 once avoidance counts only catalogue algorithms). Shown a correct program of another algorithm and told not to use it, the model goes home to its default (0.05 of attempts under the copy prompt, 0.72 under the ban), and Llama does the same on five of six present minor bans. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct mostly ignores bans, and its ban of DFS on connected components raised DFS from 29 to 43 correct programs. How often a ban is obeyed depends on its wording more than on anything else measured; the fourth template, which states only that X is not allowed here, is the weakest in every artifact, in Gemma and in Qwen2.5, where all 70 of its programs used the banned default. Bans of five names fail by reimplementation in both families tested: Qwen3-8B and Gemma write no algorithm outside the banned set (avoidance 0.00), Gemma moving from its default DFS to its minority BFS (10 to 41 of 50) at half the pass rate, with its prompt states beside a banned centroid in activation space; a push along the top-five direction breaks programs before it moves the algorithm.
lines.6204: What decides the replacement under a modal ban has measured leads and no confirmed rule. The likelihood instrument of iteration 2 cannot decide it, and substitution by the alternative the model states is not supported in Qwen3-8B. The runner-up of the base model names where a push lands in 17 of 21 recorded events across Qwen3-8B and Gemma (5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement, 3 of 3 and 3 of 4 on new tasks, 5 of 7 in Gemma), and it beats the instruct twin's teacher-forced ranking of algorithm openings 8:1 where the two disagree (p 0.020, retrospective). But where the instruct twin already writes an alternative, that alternative names the landing as often (6 of 7), and on the 8 held-out events where the twin wrote none the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053): the landing half is descriptive. The base model's own variety does not say whether a task can be moved: over 13 new units its off-default share ranks movability at Spearman 0.15 (95% interval -0.44 to 0.65; power 0.63 at a true 0.6; 0.035 if count inversions' share is taken from its correct programs), so a strong relation is excluded and a moderate one is not; only the runtime merit of the fastest alternative tracks movability after Holm correction (0.71). Both verdicts are conditional on the ban-free unit and seeds of iteration 5. Writing the task-specification states of the base model into the instruct prefill reopened the base runner-up on 1 of 5 Qwen3-8B tasks and 2 of 7 Gemma tasks, the latter where the instruct twin already wrote it 8% to 12% of the time.
lines.6206: Where a ban acts depends on the task. On the path tasks it is carried mostly by the prompt states (likelihood readout 0.85; behaviour 0.98 on the shortest path task, mixed on the grid task), and Stage A now shows the same for shortest path and kth smallest in behaviour. On the bench, pooled over five gated tasks, the direct route carries 0.744 [0.38, 1.11] of the behavioural effect and the prompt states 0.611 [0.06, 1.17], with overlapping intervals; two sum, classed as direct, also carries 0.43 of its ban in the task-specification states. The ban is enforced at the opening of the program body, to a single token on kth smallest; Gemma's natural choice falls at the same point, the first algorithm-specific statement after an opening shared by every algorithm. The read position predicts how strongly a wording will be obeyed (-0.41 across 110 wordings) but carries none of the effect when exchanged or spliced. Push movability as a forecast of which bans a model obeys is closed: inconclusive in the held-out family under its primary rule and disconfirmed under its drop sensitivity.
lines.6208: No instruction, knob, push, transplant, feature clamp or verbal edit produced a correct novel algorithm. Iterations 1 to 3 produced 116 correct programs outside the catalogue and none was new; iteration 4, none of 14,206 correct programs of the site and subspace experiments; iteration 5, none of 130 correct programs outside the catalogue. In iteration 6 a second blind adjudication of the 14 transplant programs that two of three judges had called novel, by two model families the run had not used and with ten controls of known class, found 1 novel call by one judge (a linear search, overturned on a full read) and 0 by the other, a final count of 0; the exchange experiment, the Gemma experiment (1 of 1,450 correct programs outside the catalogue) and the NLA experiment (10 correct programs labelled other) found none either. The long-form instruction of the request makes most outputs claim novelty while their code is a catalogue algorithm or absent. Within single-sample generation the reachable ideas are the model's known catalogue; search with an evaluator, which this run did not test, is the documented route to new programs [81, 82].
lines.6210: What remains open follows from this. The first question is whether the algorithm choice in Qwen3-8B is a low-rank variable at the task-specification positions: DAS fitted against the Stage A exchanges, and the projection of iteration 4's 40 directions onto the fitted subspace, would test it, and the engine control has made those directions a stable target. The second is what makes the ban-free unit weaker than the ban unit at a larger scalar dose: its per-position and per-block profile or its direction seeds. The third is whether a small push at Gemma's fork switches the algorithm without breaking the program. The fourth is whether base intent, the best knob priced so far, holds on more tasks and against plan noise at its absolute unit. Of the items of the request, the following have been run: the geometry plots in activation coordinates (at a label-dependent position in iteration 2, at the plan site in iteration 4, and for the top-five prohibition in Qwen3-8B and Gemma in iteration 6), the top-five prohibition by prompt, token veto and plan push, natural BFS against DFS internals (within a ban in Qwen3-8B, within one prompt in Gemma), thought anchors, the logit and tuned lenses, the same seed test with thinking on and off and with top-k 10, natural language autoencoders (on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), sparse autoencoders (Qwen-Scope on Qwen3-8B, Gemma Scope 2 on Gemma) and a first-order attribution in place of a circuit graph. The manifold of algorithms in a causally fitted plan subspace was planned and not run.
